title: AMD Just Had Its Biggest Run Against Nvidia Since 1999. Can It Survive Earnings?
detail:
AMD Just Had Its Biggest Run Against Nvidia Since 1999. Can It Survive Earnings?
Kamina Bashir
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 12:06 PM PST 3 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AMD outperformed Nvidia by 53.2 percentage points over five trading days, according to The Kobeissi Letter. That is the widest gap between the two chipmakers since Nvidia went public in January 1999.

That lead met its first test on Friday, when AMD stock fell 8.75%. Nvidia's November 17 earnings report now sets up the next one.

How Nvidia's Leadership Crisis Fed the AMD Rally

AMD rallied 44.7% over the 5-day stretch while Nvidia dropped 8.5%, according to The Kobeissi Letter. The previous record gap, set in April 2016, stood at 49.9 percentage points.

So far this year, the AMD vs Nvidia gap is even wider. AMD stock has gained 149.4% since January 1, while Nvidia is down 12.7%, as of Friday's close. That puts the year-to-date gap at about 162 percentage points.

Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens

The run overlapped with growing scrutiny of Jensen Huang, who quit Nvidia as CEO on November 12. The company named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent replacement.

AMD also gave buyers its own numbers to work with. Its third-quarter revenue rose 45% from a year earlier to a record $13.4 billion. Data center sales nearly doubled to $8.5 billion.

"AMD has been a major beneficiary of Nvidia's historic volatility," The Kobeissi Letter posted on X.

Friday's Sell-Off Hands the Next Move to Nvidia

The record run lost some ground in Friday's session. AMD closed at $534.06, down from $585.30, and slipped another 2.41% to $521.20 after hours.

AMD Stock Performance. Source: Google Finance

Chip stocks sold off as a group. The 10-year Treasury yield remained above 5% after October's producer price index. Rising yields tend to hit growth stocks hardest, since their value rests on profits expected years ahead.

Trading volume reached 48.6 million shares, nearly double the 3-month average. Analysts at The Motley Fool linked part of the drop to profit-taking after the surge.

The after-hours price now sits just above $514. BeInCrypto's AMD stock price analysis marked that level as the line that would break the bullish setup.

Nvidia earnings land on Tuesday after the US market closes. The company guided for $108 billion in third-quarter revenue, plus or minus 2%. Analysts polled by LSEG expect about $109.2 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.48 per share.

The quarter closed on October 25, before Huang resigned, so the results will reflect his tenure. The guidance for the next quarter will be the first issued with Kress as interim CEO.

Solid results and guidance could draw investors back to Nvidia. A weak one could drag the whole chip group lower, AMD included, because Friday showed both stocks still trade together.

Why Advanced Micro Devices Stock Surged This Week
Howard Smith, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 5:06 AM PST 4 min read
AMD
^GSPC
CRWV
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A major host-infrastructure deal with Google Cloud, alongside expanding data center demand, sent Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) soaring 19% this week.

Advanced Micro Devices stock changed hands at $534.06 as of Friday's close, adding about 19% from Friday, Nov. 6's close. Over the same period, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) rose 2.5%, and the Nasdaq-100 was up 2.4%.

Image source: Getty Images.

Data center wins and cloud deals drive market momentum

The rally gained traction after AI cloud provider CoreWeave reported strong quarterly results and raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $37 billion to $39 billion, increasing the lower end of the range. That massive infrastructure spending plan reassures investors that tech companies continue buying data center processors at a rapid pace. At the same time, Google Cloud announced that AMD's 5th Gen EPYC server processors will power the host infrastructure for its new confidential computing systems, reinforcing AMD's market share gains in enterprise computing.

Advanced Micro Devices designs computer processors and graphics chips and sells data center servers and PC components to cloud providers and computer manufacturers that build high-performance systems. The company's EPYC line of server microprocessors powers cloud data centers, while its Instinct graphics processors handle complex artificial intelligence workloads. Winning major cloud deployments expands AMD's addressable market beyond traditional personal computers and positions its hardware at the foundation of modern cloud infrastructure.

In its last reported quarter, which ended Sept. 26, 2026, AMD generated $13.4 billion in revenue, up 45% year over year, while data center sales nearly doubled to $8.5 billion. Fresh data center deals and competitive shifts invert concerns over market share losses, establishing AMD as an indispensable alternative supplier for large-scale artificial intelligence infrastructure.

High expectations leave little room for error

AMD stock trades at a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 117.6. That rich valuation reflects high market expectations for sustained earnings growth as cloud providers ramp up processor orders.

Investors will closely watch Nvidia's upcoming quarterly report and AMD's next earnings release on Feb. 2, 2027, to confirm whether data center hardware demand maintains its trajectory. Any slowdown in hyperscaler capital budgets could quickly compress AMD's elevated valuation multiple.

Key Takeaways

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on November 12, and chip stocks like AMD and Broadcom fell sharply. That puts Arista Networks' pitch of working with many chip vendors in the spotlight.

Arista's third-quarter revenue rose 58.5% to $3.66 billion, its fastest growth since its IPO, and management guided 2027 revenue to about $18.5 billion.

Non-GAAP gross margin slipped to 64.0% from 65.2%, while two customers made up 42% of Arista's 2025 revenue.

Nvidia's report next week, its first under interim CEO Colette Kress, is the next read on AI networking demand before Arista reports in February.

Nvidia (NVDA) lost its founder as chief executive this week, and the whole AI hardware trade felt it.

On November 12, the company said Jensen Huang had resigned, with CFO Colette Kress stepping in as interim CEO. By Friday afternoon, the Philadelphia semiconductor index was down 4%, and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) and Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ) were sharply lower.

Arista Networks (ANET:NYSE) sits right in the middle of that trade. Nvidia competes with it in AI Ethernet switching, while AMD and Broadcom helped it launch new open AI racks last quarter.

So the question is simple. Does a shakeup at Nvidia hurt Arista, or does it make Arista's open, multi-vendor pitch look smarter?

Arista's record quarter in numbers

Arista reported on November 3, and its growth was the fastest since its IPO.

Revenue rose 58.5% to $3.66 billion, well above its own $3.3 billion guidance.

Non-GAAP EPS reached $1.20, up from $0.77 a year earlier.

Operating margin on a non-GAAP basis improved to 49.1% from 48.6%.

CEO Jayshree Ullal said the quarter came in "surpassing even my high expectations." Product sales did the heavy lifting…

Arista Networks (ANET): product and service revenue, quarterly, $ millions, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

Product revenue grew 66.9% to $3.19 billion, while services grew 17.9%. Fourth-quarter guidance of $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion implies about 8% more sequential growth at the midpoint.

A bet on every accelerator

Arista's pitch is that AI clusters will run on many kinds of accelerators, and every one of them needs a network.

Last quarter it launched open, liquid-cooled rack designs with AMD, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Qualcomm and others. Its Etherlink SU-144 rack links up to 144 accelerators in a single hop.

That strategy shows up in the 2027 plan. On its earnings call, management guided revenue up 38% to 40%, to about $18.5 billion. It also expects AI networking revenue to double to roughly $7 billion.

Nvidia, though, is still growing much faster at the top line.

Arista Networks vs. Nvidia (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): revenue growth YoY (%), quarterly, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

In its July quarter, Nvidia's data center revenue jumped 117% to $89.0 billion, and its Spectrum-X Ethernet sales grew 2.6 times. A distracted Nvidia could open doors for Arista, but one week of headlines won't prove it.

What this means for investors

AMD stock was up as much as 30% this week, and still ended the week with solid gains, despite today's decline. AMD investors shouldn't be overly concerned with how the stock performed Friday. It was caught in the downdraft stemming from uncertainty surrounding Nvidia in its post-Jensen Huang era.

Last week, AMD reported third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion and said data-center sales nearly doubled year over year. The strong outlook for its data center segment, along with similar comments from other AI-related names this week, helped the stock before today's pullback.

AMD could benefit from Nvidia's internal struggles, but investors should continue to focus on AMD's underlying business strength. As long as the AI-related data center growth continues, the company looks to have a long growth runway.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) fell 9% today, giving back part of the roughly 30% it gained this week after Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) CEO Jensen Huang resigned.

AMD put out no news of its own, and investors sold the whole chip group, Marvell Technology (MRVL:NASDAQ), Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) and Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) included.

Easy come, easy go

Huang resigned on Thursday, and investors piled into AMD as the obvious alternative. Today some of that money went back out.

Nvidia fell 2% after HSBC cut it to Hold. The 10-year yield also hit 5.17% after a hot wholesale inflation reading, and higher yields hurt stocks priced on profits years out.

Nobody got a pass

Marvell fell 5% with no news of its own. It agreed to buy Lumentum on Nov. 2 and said its fiscal third-quarter revenue was in line with guidance, so its Dec. 1 report is its chance to show the selling was about the group.

The server CPU makers fell together, too: Intel slipped 3% and Arm 5%. UBS's Timothy Arcuri estimates third-quarter server CPU shipments rose 31% from a year earlier, with Arm's unit share up to 20.1%, Intel's down to 51.5% and AMD's roughly flat at 28.4%. When all three fall at once, investors are questioning how long that market keeps growing.

title: Better Chip Stock: Nvidia vs. AMD
detail:
Better Chip Stock: Nvidia vs. AMD
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 1:43 PM PST 5 min read
NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) shareholders have had a rough few days. After a week in which news broke that CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman who is accused of being a Chinese spy, and another with an Nvidia executive, on Thursday morning, he resigned.

The exit of the man who has been the face of the company for decades has investors worried about its future. AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) shareholders aren't in the same boat, and the chipmaker is enjoying surging data center sales.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

However, the question remains: Which stock is the better buy? It's a hard question to answer, because at face value, Nvidia is doing far better than AMD. But AMD doesn't have other questions surrounding the state of its business.

What matters is what you value most as an investor, as Nvidia is likely to be a tumultuous stock to own over the next few months.

Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia is still winning the AI processor race

Before comparing Nvidia and AMD stocks, investors must answer a different question: How capable will Nvidia be without Huang in the CEO role? If you're of the view that the company's future really rests on the caliber of the person in the top job, then Nvidia's investment thesis can't be properly analyzed until his permanent successor is picked. For now, respected CFO Colette Kress occupies the role on an interim basis.

If it doesn't matter to you who is leading Nvidia, then you're free to proceed to the next point.

Nvidia and AMD are both computing unit designers, although their businesses look a bit different. AMD's product lineup is a lot broader than Nvidia's, and so is its customer base. It has sizable businesses in the consumer electronics world as well as in embedded processors and data centers. However, almost all investors care about is the data center business, as that's what is growing rapidly right now.

During Q3, AMD's data center revenue rose 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. That's a strong result, and investors are excited. However, because AMD also has fairly large exposure to other segments, its overall growth rate was 45%, bringing its top line to $13.4 billion. The problem is it isn't anywhere close to Nvidia's growth and size.

Nvidia reports its fiscal 2027 Q3 results on Nov. 17. But until we get that update about the recent state of the business, the best we can do is to use its fiscal Q2 results. In that period, its data center sales rose 117% year over year to $89 billion. Because Nvidia's data center business makes up a far larger chunk of its total, Nvidia's overall revenue growth rate was 106% to $96.2 billion.

First, I think it's important to put AMD's remarkable triple-digit rally this year into context. I see two key metrics that have marked a turning point in the company's investment thesis: Data Center revenue growth and forward revenue growth.

Let's start by breaking down the first metric. Basically, the market has gone from viewing AMD as a central processing unit (CPU) manufacturer trying to gain ground in artificial intelligence (AI) graphics processing units (GPUs) to treating it as a potential second major AI infrastructure platform, behind Nvidia (NVDA).

The acceleration driven by AI demand really began to show up in AMD's results in 2026, something that wasn't nearly as pronounced in 2025. To be more specific, in the third quarter of 2025, AMD generated $4.34 billion in Data Center revenue, up 22% year-over-year. A year later, that revenue reached $8.55 billion, a 97% jump, driven by both EPYC processors, benefiting particularly from the growth of AI agents, and Instinct MI450 GPUs. As a result, Data Center now accounts for 64% of the company's total revenue, compared to less than 50% in the same period last year.

As if that weren't enough, this growth came with a considerable improvement in the segment's profitability. Data Center's operating margin rose from 25% to 34%. So, we're talking about a company whose core business has nearly doubled in size while its margins have expanded by an impressive 9 percentage points.
